reference.source: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye / Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: Presents with grittiness, burning, foreign body sensation, fluctuating vision, and paradoxical reflex tearing
Broadly divided into aqueous-deficient (reduced tear production) and evaporative (mostly meibomian gland dysfunction) types, though many patients have mixed disease
Symptoms often exceed clinical signs, and vision that clears on blinking is characteristic
Useful clinical tests include tear film break-up time, ocular surface staining with fluorescein or lissamine green, and the Schirmer test
Aqueous-deficient dry eye may signal Sjogren syndrome, so ask about dry mouth and joint symptoms
A stepwise management approach begins with lubricants, lid hygiene, and environmental measures, escalating to anti-inflammatory therapy, punctal occlusion, and secretagogues
Meibomian gland dysfunction is managed with warm compresses, lid hygiene, and treatment of associated blepharitis and rosacea
Untreated severe disease can cause filamentary keratitis, persistent epithelial defects, and, rarely, corneal melting or perforation
reference.pathophysiology: Dry eye disease is a multifactorial disorder of the ocular surface characterised by loss of tear film homeostasis. Reduced aqueous production (as in Sjogren and non-Sjogren lacrimal dysfunction) or excessive evaporation (chiefly from meibomian gland dysfunction with an unstable lipid layer) leads to tear hyperosmolarity. Hyperosmolarity triggers a self-perpetuating cycle of ocular surface inflammation, epithelial damage, and neurosensory dysfunction, which further destabilises the tear film. Goblet cell loss and reduced mucin worsen wetting, sustaining the inflammatory cascade.
additionalDifferentials: Corneal epithelial disease or recurrent erosion
additionalInvestigations: Tear film break-up time to assess tear stability
Ocular surface staining with fluorescein and lissamine green
Schirmer test to quantify aqueous production
Autoantibody and systemic testing when Sjogren syndrome is suspected
redFlags: Persistent epithelial defect, corneal thinning, or melt indicating severe surface breakdown
Features of Sjogren syndrome or other systemic autoimmune disease requiring investigation
Marked reduction in corneal sensation suggesting neurotrophic keratopathy
Rapidly worsening pain, photophobia, or infiltrate suggesting secondary infection
reference.prognosis: Dry eye disease is usually chronic and requires ongoing management; most patients achieve good symptom control, but severe or autoimmune-associated disease can cause persistent surface damage and visual impairment.
pitfalls: Focusing on aqueous supplementation while neglecting meibomian gland dysfunction and lid disease
Overlooking underlying Sjogren syndrome in aqueous-deficient patients
Attributing all irritation to dryness and missing allergy, infection, or medication toxicity
Long-term use of preserved drops aggravating ocular surface toxicity
